choices: Tell the caller to check the documentation, then hang up and handle the outage ticket immediately since it affects more people.
Stay on the call, acknowledge the frustration, take ownership of a next step with a specific time, and route the outage ticket to a teammate or the on-call queue while staying with the caller.
Promise the caller you will fix it in the next ten minutes even though you have not diagnosed it yet, so you can get to the outage.
Escalate the caller to a manager immediately so you are free to work the outage ticket yourself.
desc: An angry customer is stuck on your line while another SLA clock runs down.
hint: Which option keeps both issues owned and moving without breaking the process or making empty promises?
prompt: What is the MOST effective response?
situation: A customer calls, furious that their payroll export has been broken for two days. They are raising their voice and demanding the fix 'right now.' While you are on the phone, you see another ticket hit a 30-minute SLA for an outage affecting fifty users. The customer's issue, from a first glance, looks like a misconfiguration they could have avoided, not a platform bug.
title: The Furious Caller and the Tickling Clock
why: The best answer de-escalates with empathy, commits to a concrete next step rather than an impossible promise, and keeps both tickets moving by routing the outage through the proper queue instead of abandoning either customer. Dropping the caller for the outage trades one breach for another and burns trust; promising an undiagnosed ten-minute fix sets up a second broken promise; and escalating a customer you have not yet attempted to help is over-escalation that wastes a lead's time.

choices: Quietly move their ticket to the front of the queue; renewals matter and nobody will audit the order.
Ignore the direct email and let them re-submit through the queue so they learn the process.

Respond promptly, open a ticket on their behalf with the correct priority per the SLA matrix, acknowledge their urgency, and offer to escalate through the proper channel if the business impact warrants re-prioritization.
Tell them the renewal comment is inappropriate and that their ticket will be handled in standard order as a consequence.
desc: A large account contact demands to jump the support queue.
hint: Fairness to every customer in the queue is part of the job — how do you honor both urgency and process?
prompt: What is the MOST effective response?
situation: A contact at your company's biggest account emails you directly, bypassing the ticket queue, demanding an engineer look at a 'production-blocking' issue today. Your SLA says P3 tickets from enterprise accounts get a 4-hour response, and the queue currently has twelve tickets ahead of them. The contact hints that their renewal is up for discussion next quarter.
title: The VIP Who Skips the Line
why: Creating the ticket properly, validating urgency against the SLA matrix, and using the official escalation path serves the customer fast while keeping queue fairness and an audit trail intact. Secretly jumping the line erodes team trust and SLA credibility for everyone else; ignoring them is avoidance that risks a real production issue; and punishing them for the renewal remark injects personal judgment and blame into a service relationship.

choices: Make the config change yourself now, then file the change ticket afterward so the SLA does not breach.
Tell the customer nothing until you have a final fix, to avoid worrying them.

Send an honest update: describe what you found, what the proper next steps are, who owns the change, and the realistic timeline; ask the owning team for an expedited review per process, and document the workaround for approval.
Blame the other team's change process for the delay so the customer's manager directs pressure at them.
desc: SLA is about to breach on a ticket with a risky shortcut available.
hint: SLA pressure never justifies skipping change control — what path restores service fastest WITHOUT breaking process?
objectives: Meet the SLA if safely possible
prompt: What is the MOST effective response?
situation: A customer ticket is at 85% of its SLA. You found a workaround that would restore their service today, but it requires editing a production config that is owned by another team and normally needs a change ticket plus a 24-hour review. The customer's manager is CC'd and asking for an update every hour.
title: The Workaround vs. the Deadline
why: Transparent status, a documented workaround routed through expedited-but-legitimate review, and clear ownership keep the customer informed and protect production integrity. A silent config edit is hero work that bypasses controls and risks a wider outage; going silent until the fix is ready is avoidance that lets the SLA clock expire unaddressed; and blaming the owning team destroys the cross-team trust needed for the expedite.

choices: Send it as-is; accuracy matters more than tone, and the customer really is not following instructions.

Rewrite the reply to remove the condescension, acknowledge the customer's effort, offer a live walkthrough instead of another text list, and suggest to your teammate that repeated failures signal the instructions need improving.
Delete the draft and send the customer a link to the knowledge base article instead.
Reply privately to the teammate criticizing their tone and leave the ticket untouched until they respond.
desc: A draft reply to a confused customer is technically accurate but hostile in tone.
hint: Three failed attempts point at the instructions, not the customer — what fixes the message AND the root cause?
prompt: What is the MOST effective response?
situation: A customer has reopened the same ticket three times, each time missing a step from your instructions. A teammate drafts a reply that is technically correct but reads as condescending: 'As stated previously, you need to follow the steps exactly as written.' The teammate asks you to review it before sending. The customer is already frustrated and the ticket is aging.
title: The Blunt Email
why: A rewritten, empathetic reply plus a live walkthrough resolves the immediate case, while flagging the instructions as the pattern fixes the root cause for the next customer. Sending a hostile-but-accurate reply burns the relationship; swapping in a KB link the customer already failed with repeats the same loop; and sidelining the ticket to lecture a teammate leaves the customer waiting and the problem unsolved.

choices: Work them in ticket-number order to be fair to everyone.
Jump on the VPN ticket first since it is the only one you are certain you can finish today.

Verify the disk-fill alert first since a shared-server outage would dwarf both other issues, then tackle the finance report given its time-bounded business impact, update each ticket with your reasoning, and queue the VPN issue with notes for the next shift.
Escalate all three to your lead so they decide the order for you.
desc: You must sequence three competing tickets with conflicting claims of urgency.
hint: Priority labels are inputs, not orders — what would a real outage cost versus the other two?
objectives: Validate priority labels, not just accept them
prompt: What is the MOST effective response?
situation: You have 90 minutes left in your shift. Three tickets are open: (A) a single user's VPN issue marked P4 by the intake queue; (B) a P2 finance reconciliation report that is wrong and blocking month-end close, claimed urgent by the requester but not marked higher; (C) a monitoring alert that looks like a slow disk fill on a shared server, currently informational severity. Your instinct says C could become an outage, but it is not paging anyone yet.
title: Three Tickets, One Engineer
why: Checking the credible-outage signal first, then the time-bounded business impact, then documenting the queue is prioritization by real risk and impact, with a clean trail for the next shift. Ticket-number order ignores impact entirely; doing the easy ticket first is avoidance dressed as productivity; and escalating routine sequencing to a lead is abdication that wastes their time.

choices: Drop your migration and review the plan; being a team player matters more than one deadline.
Say you are too busy and brush them off without offering anything.
Be direct: explain your deadline constraint, offer a bounded slot today or a fuller review tomorrow, and point them to the runbook or another reviewer who has capacity.
Agree to the review but do it half-heartedly while keeping your migration window open, so neither gets your full attention.
desc: An urgent interruption competes with a committed project deadline.
hint: A flat yes burns your deadline; a flat no burns the relationship — what's the third option?
objectives: Help the colleague without derailing yourself
prompt: What is the MOST effective response?
situation: You are deep into a migration task with a deadline your team committed to for tomorrow morning. A colleague from another team stops by your desk and asks you to urgently review their deployment plan because their window is tonight and 'it will only take twenty minutes.' You know from experience their twenty minutes is usually ninety. Your manager is in meetings all afternoon.
title: The Tap on the Shoulder
why: Naming the constraint, offering a concrete bounded alternative, and redirecting to another reviewer protects the committed deadline while still moving the colleague forward. Dropping a committed deliverable for an unplanned request breaks a promise your team made; brushing them off damages collaboration; and splitting attention guarantees both outcomes are worse.

choices: Do the director's task first because budget power outranks your manager.
Do your manager's task and ignore the director, since chain of command is clear.

Tell both stakeholders about the conflict plainly, give each the realistic effort estimate, and ask your manager to make the priority call — then execute the decision and keep the other party updated.
Work late and do both silently so nobody is disappointed.
desc: Two stakeholders both claim their request is the top priority.
hint: Picking a winner yourself is politics; working yourself into burnout is silent heroics — who actually owns priority decisions?
prompt: What is the MOST effective response?
situation: Your direct manager asked you this morning to finish a security-patch audit by end of day. At lunch, a director from another department — who controls budget your team relies on — asks you to 'just quickly' pull usage analytics for a board deck due tomorrow, implying it should come first. Both say their task is the priority. You have capacity for roughly one of them before end of day.
title: Two Bosses, One Afternoon
why: Surfacing the conflict with honest estimates and letting your manager decide is how priorities get resolved legitimately, and updating both sides preserves the relationships either way. Ranking by budget power is politicking outside your authority; defaulting to chain of command without disclosure leaves the director blindsided; and silently overworking hides the capacity problem and sets an unsustainable precedent.

choices: Take the feature; the sponsor is watching and the database issue has no complaints attached.
Quietly fix the database on the side without telling anyone, and do the feature too.
Raise the brownout connection with the team and product owner, present the trade-off with the outage risk stated plainly, and let the sprint decision be made with full information.
Block the feature unilaterally, declaring the database fix an emergency.
desc: A hidden reliability problem competes with visible feature work.
hint: The right call isn't picking one — it's making sure the decision is made with the outage risk on the table.
prompt: What is the MOST effective response?
situation: Your sprint has two candidate items and room for one: a customer-facing dashboard feature the sales team is demoing next week, and a database index fix you discovered that would prevent the slow queries behind last month's two brownouts. The brownouts were never root-caused publicly, and the feature has an executive sponsor watching it. No customer is complaining about the queries right now.
title: The Quiet Rot
why: Bringing the hidden risk into the open lets the team and product owner weigh a real outage against a demo deadline with eyes open — prioritization with full information. Taking the feature alone buries a known risk for optics; a stealth side-fix is unreviewed hero work that hides the trade-off; and unilaterally blocking the feature is authority you do not have.

choices: Roll back yesterday's deploy immediately; it is the most likely cause and speed matters most.
Wait for the secondary to wake up before doing anything, to avoid making it worse.

Declare the incident, open the incident channel, page the secondary through the escalation policy, verify the failure scope with quick checks, and update the status page — investigate before changing production.
Spend the next hour digging through logs alone until you are certain of the cause, then act.
desc: An outage fires and you are the first responder with incomplete information.
hint: Discipline beats speed in the first fifteen minutes — what creates shared visibility and a proper escalation?
objectives: Avoid acting on hunches in production
prompt: What is the MOST effective response?
situation: At 2:40 AM you get paged: the customer portal is returning errors for all users. The runbook's first step is to check the status page, which says all green. Your secondary on-call is not answering their phone. You have a partial hunch it is the auth service, based on a deploy that went out yesterday evening, but you cannot prove it yet.
title: You Are the First Pager
why: Declaring the incident, paging through the escalation policy, scoping the failure, and updating the status page create coordination and visibility without gambling on an unproven hunch. Rolling back on a hunch can cause a second outage; waiting passively for one person abandons the incident; and lone-wolfing for an hour leaves customers and teammates in the dark.

choices: Restart everything as the VP asked; they outrank the incident commander.
Tell the VP to leave the channel so the team can work.

Have the incident commander (or you, if they delegate) give a brief status with what is known, what is being tested, and the next update time — and explain plainly why the suggested restart is unsafe right now, offering the safer alternative being pursued.
Give an optimistic ETA you cannot support to get the VP out of the channel.
desc: Leadership joins the incident channel demanding faster resolution.
hint: Rank doesn't change blast radius — how do you give leadership what they need without breaking the response?
prompt: What is the MOST effective response?
situation: During an active SEV-2, a VP joins the incident channel and asks for 'an ETA on the fix in the next five minutes' and suggests 'just restarting everything.' The incident commander is mid-diagnosis. You are a responder with the best current picture of the failure. The restart the VP suggests would drop in-flight transactions.
title: The Exec in the Channel
why: A crisp status with known facts, active hypotheses, and a next-update time gives leadership confidence while the plain explanation of the restart's risk keeps production safe. Obeying the VP's shortcut would cause data loss; ordering a VP out of the channel is disrespectful and escalates the wrong conflict; and fabricating an ETA trades short-term calm for a second broken promise.

choices: Agree that the engineer was careless; accountability means consequences for mistakes.
Shut down the discussion entirely and end the meeting early to protect the engineer.

Redirect to the system: note that a runbook layout which makes prod-vs-staging easy to confuse is a process failure, refocus on guardrails (confirmation prompts, environment labeling, dry-run defaults), and affirm that blameless means fixing conditions, not punishing people.
Let the privilege-removal vote happen since the majority supports it.
desc: A postmortem threatens to become a blame session after a human-error outage.
hint: Blameless doesn't mean consequence-free systems — it means the question is 'how did this become possible,' not 'who did it.'
objectives: Fix the system that allowed the error
prompt: What is the MOST effective response?
situation: Yesterday's outage was caused by an engineer running a migration script against production instead of staging — a mistake the runbook layout arguably invited. In the postmortem, several attendees start framing it as 'carelessness' and someone suggests the engineer should lose deploy privileges. You were the incident commander.
title: The Postmortem Finger-Point
why: Refocusing on the runbook's ambiguity and concrete guardrails produces fixes that protect every future engineer, while affirming blameless norms keeps the team honest in the next incident. Punishing the engineer teaches everyone to hide mistakes; ending the meeting dodges the real work; and a majority vote for punishment is blame with a democratic veneer.

choices: Post that it is likely the third-party provider's fault; it calms customers and might be true.
Keep posting 'investigating' with no new detail until the cause is fully confirmed.
Publish a fuller honest update: scope of impact, what has been ruled out, what is being tested now, what customers can do meanwhile, and the next update time — without speculating on blame.
Stop updating the status page so customers stop replying angrily.
desc: Customers demand answers while the cause is still unknown.
hint: Customers can handle bad news better than vague news — and they remember who blamed a partner without proof.
prompt: What is the MOST effective response?
situation: A partial outage is affecting roughly a third of API traffic. You have ruled out the usual suspects but the cause is still unknown after 40 minutes. The support team says customers are furious about the generic 'we are investigating' updates. Someone suggests posting that it is 'likely a third-party provider issue' to buy goodwill, since the provider had a blip this morning.
title: The Status Page Dilemma
why: A substantive, blame-free update with ruled-outs, active tests, and a next-update time respects customers and keeps trust even mid-outage. Blaming the provider on a hunch risks a public false accusation; repeating an empty 'investigating' starves customers of useful information; and going silent is avoidance that reads as indifference.

choices: Approve it to keep the peace; the sprint goal matters and the bug may never trigger.
Escalate to the tech lead immediately, framing the peer as rushing unsafe code.
Write a small reproduction or test demonstrating the race, share it calmly with the peer, and propose a concrete fix or a paired session — keeping the discussion on the code, not the person.
Refuse to review any of their future PRs until they take your feedback seriously.
desc: You and a peer disagree sharply in a code review.
hint: Evidence ends opinion wars — what moves the debate from 'theoretical' to decided?
prompt: What is the MOST effective response?
situation: You left review comments on a peer's pull request flagging a race condition you are fairly confident about. The peer pushed back hard, calling your concern 'theoretical' and asking you to approve so they hit their sprint goal. Two other teammates have stayed silent. The change touches shared infrastructure code.
title: The Review Standoff
why: A reproduction turns a standoff into a technical fact and a paired session keeps the relationship collaborative while protecting shared code. Rubber-stamping for harmony risks a real production bug; escalating with a character framing poisons trust; and boycotting their reviews is retaliation that hurts the whole team.

choices: Tell your lead the previous owner did a terrible job and that Friday is impossible.
Silently work nights to hit Friday and never mention the missing context.

Reconstruct what you can from commits and logs, timebox the archaeology, give your lead an honest status with a revised estimate, and ask the former teammate one focused set of questions — framing it as a handoff gap to fix, not a person to blame.
Restart the migration from scratch without reading their work, to avoid inheriting their mistakes.
desc: A departing teammate leaves you a half-finished task with no context.
hint: Blame doesn't write docs and heroics don't scale — what gives your lead a real plan?
prompt: What is the MOST effective response?
situation: A teammate who rotated off your project left a half-finished data migration in your lap: no docs, cryptic commit messages, and a Slack thread that ends mid-discussion. The migration is due Friday. The teammate is now on a different team and slow to respond. Your lead asks for a status update today.
title: The Messy Handoff
why: Timeboxed archaeology plus an honest status and a focused question set gives the lead a real estimate and treats the gap as a process problem to fix for next time. Trash-talking the departed teammate burns a bridge and excuses nothing; silent overwork hides the risk until Friday; and a from-scratch rewrite discards real progress on a hunch.

choices: Refuse the page and let the alert fire until the other team accepts ownership.
Handle the immediate incident yourself tonight, document the routing gap and the refused handoff factually, and raise it in the morning with both leads to fix ownership and alert routing permanently.
Fix the alert routing yourself at 2 AM by editing the paging config, then go back to sleep.
Complain about the other team's on-call in the shared channel while the alert is still firing.
desc: On-call friction erupts when a page lands in the wrong rotation.
hint: Ownership arguments don't lower error rates — what sequence stops the bleeding AND ends the monthly repeat?
objectives: Fix the routing ownership for real
prompt: What is the MOST effective response?
situation: You get paged at 1 AM for a service your team handed off to another team last month. The alert routing was never updated. The other team's on-call says it is still your team's service and refuses to take it. The alert is real — error rates are climbing. You are exhausted and this is the third misrouted page this month.
title: The Page That Wasn't Yours
why: Responding to the live incident first protects customers, and a factual morning follow-up with both leads fixes the routing and ownership dispute permanently. Refusing the page lets an outage burn over a turf war; editing paging config half-asleep risks making routing worse; and venting in the shared channel escalates personalities instead of solving the gap.

choices: Stay silent; the lead is senior and the team seems on board.
Call out the flaw bluntly in front of everyone so the mistake is stopped immediately.

Raise it as a question tied to the shared goal: ask how the plan handles sync with the other team's existing store, offer the alternative you see, and volunteer to check with that team — disagreeing with the idea while respecting the person.
Go to the lead's manager afterward to report that the lead's plan is flawed.
desc: Your tech lead's plan has a flaw you can see but they can't yet.
hint: Silence protects egos, bluntness protects nobody — how do you put the risk on the table without making it personal?
prompt: What is the MOST effective response?
situation: Your tech lead proposes an architecture for a new integration in the team meeting, and you spot a real problem: it duplicates a data store that another team already maintains, which will cause sync conflicts. The lead is senior, well-liked, and clearly excited about the plan. Everyone else in the meeting is nodding along.
title: Pushing Back on the Lead
why: Framing the concern as a question about a shared goal surfaces the real risk, invites the lead's own expertise into the fix, and keeps the meeting collaborative. Silence lets a foreseeable sync-conflict ship; a blunt public takedown embarrasses the lead and makes the next disagreement harder; and going to their manager is escalation past the person who could have resolved it in the room.
